questions: Are you fully aware of your surroundings during these movements?
Did these movements begin after you were given a medication for nausea, vomiting, or psychosis?
Do you have painful muscle spasms triggered by touch, sound, or movement?
Have you had a recent wound, especially a puncture wound?
Can you briefly suppress or stop the movements when you try?
Do you feel an uncomfortable urge or inner restlessness that is relieved by moving?
Do the movements disappear completely when you are asleep?
Did the movements start suddenly within the last few days?
Have you recently used, stopped, or withdrawn from alcohol, opioids, stimulants, or sedative medications?
Do you have weakness, numbness, or loss of coordination on one side of your body?
Do you have a parent, sibling, or child with Huntington disease or unexplained progressive involuntary movements?
Have you had progressive personality change, depression, irritability, memory problems, or impaired judgment over the past several months or years?
Have you recently had a sore throat or other infection followed by joint pains, rash, or involuntary movements?
Have you had episodes of confusion, seizures, memory loss, or abnormal behavior?
Have you had weight loss, darkening of the skin, persistent nausea or vomiting, dizziness on standing, or unusual salt craving?
Have you been drinking excessive amounts of water or taking diuretics or other medicines before these movements began?
Have you had a recent pregnancy, miscarriage, or childbirth?
orders: Bedside neurological examination including assessment of tone, reflexes, strength, sensation, coordination, eye movements, and characterization of the involuntary movements during distraction and voluntary tasks
Serum electrolytes including sodium, potassium, calcium, magnesium, phosphate, bicarbonate, glucose, renal function, and liver enzymes
Complete blood count, creatine kinase, thyroid-stimulating hormone, vitamin B12, and copper/ceruloplasmin levels
Urine toxicology screen including stimulants, cocaine, opioids, and sedative-hypnotics
Brain MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging of the basal ganglia
EEG, including video-EEG monitoring, to assess for epileptiform activity or an encephalopathic pattern
Lumbar puncture with cerebrospinal-fluid cell count, protein, glucose, oligoclonal bands, IgG index, and microbiological studies
Serum and CSF autoimmune encephalitis antibody panel, specifically including anti–NMDA receptor (GluN1), LGI1, CASPR2, GABA-B, AMPA, and DPPX antibodies
Pelvic ultrasound or pelvic MRI to evaluate for an ovarian teratoma
Serum cortisol and ACTH, serum and urine osmolality, and urine sodium to characterize the hyponatremia and exclude endocrine causes
Contrast-enhanced MRI of the pituitary and hypothalamus, including dedicated sellar sequences, to evaluate for pituitary or hypothalamic structural disease
Measure serum 8 AM cortisol, free T4, TSH, IGF-1, LH, FSH, estradiol, and repeat ACTH and prolactin
Dynamic ACTH (cosyntropin) stimulation test, with cortisol measured at baseline, 30 minutes, and 60 minutes
Serum antidiuretic hormone (copeptin, if available) and urine osmolality with urine sodium obtained simultaneously with serum osmolality and sodium
served: deep tendon reflexes and plantar responses
effect of voluntary action and anxiety
CSF oligoclonal bands and IgG index
morning cortisol, ACTH and pituitary hormones
